country.name: Switzerland
country.tagline: Terraced lakeshores and Alpine valleys where Chasselas, Petite Arvine and Cornalin grow almost nowhere else, and the Swiss drink nearly all of it.

stats.note: Federal Office for Agriculture (FOAG) via swissinfo.ch: 82 million litres harvested in 2025 from 14,432 ha. OIV puts Swiss consumption at 2.3 mhl in 2025, so imports dominate.

country.overview:
Switzerland has about 14,400 hectares of vines, less than the Rheingau and Mosel combined, spread across all 26 cantons but concentrated in the French-speaking west and the Italian-speaking south. Its wine is almost a secret: the Swiss drink nearly all of it, exports are a tiny share, and the country imports about two thirds of what it consumes. Yet within that small output are some of the most spectacular vineyards in Europe and a set of grapes found almost nowhere else.

The landscape does the work. Vines cling to terraces above Lake Geneva in Lavaux (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007), climb the sun-baked slopes of the Rhône valley in the Valais to over 1,100 metres at Visperterminen, line the Jura lakes of Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten, and grow on the pergolas and hills of Ticino. Lakes and mountains create warm pockets: in the Valais the Alps block rain and the föhn wind dries the slopes, making it one of the sunniest and driest places in Switzerland. Many of the finest vineyards are so steep that they are worked by hand, monorail and even helicopter.

Chasselas is the white grape that defines western Switzerland, especially Vaud. It is neutral on its own but takes on the character of place so clearly that Swiss growers treat it the way Burgundians treat Chardonnay: Dézaley tastes different from Yvorne, and a well-kept Chasselas can age for decades. Pinot Noir is the most planted grape overall, from the Bündner Herrschaft in Graubünden to Neuchâtel and the Valais, and Gamay, Merlot (the grape of Ticino since the early twentieth century) and Müller-Thurgau follow. The Valais alone has dozens of varieties, including the native or Alpine Petite Arvine, Amigne, Humagne Blanche, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Heida (Savagnin).

Swiss wine law delegates appellations to the cantons. Geneva introduced the first cantonal AOC rules in the late 1980s, the Valais introduced a quality hierarchy in 1990, and today each canton runs one or more AOCs, some with Grand Cru or Premier Grand Cru levels. The result is local and sometimes confusing (Fendant is Valais Chasselas, Dôle a Pinot-Gamay blend, Johannisberg is Sylvaner), but it maps closely onto the country's patchwork of languages and cantons.

Pressures are real. The area under vine has fallen slowly for decades, and federal support was needed in 2024 and 2025 as cheap imports and falling consumption squeezed prices. The 2025 harvest of 82 million litres was up 9 percent from a small 2024 but about 9 million litres below the ten-year average, and growers in Ticino fought an invasion of Japanese beetle. The quality, on all accounts, was excellent.

history.title: A Celtic wine bottle in the Valais
history.text: A ceramic bottle found in a Celtic tomb at Sembrancher in the Valais, dated to the second century BC, is the oldest evidence of wine in Switzerland.

history.title: Romans bring the vine
history.text: Roman settlements at Aventicum (Avenches), Octodurus (Martigny) and around Lake Geneva spread viticulture. Some Valais grapes, perhaps Amigne and Rèze, may descend from vines of that era.

history.title: Monks terrace Lavaux
history.text: Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries, with the bishops of Lausanne, built the first terraces of Lavaux; the Cistercians of Hautcrêt and Montheron shaped the Dézaley.

history.title: First Fête des Vignerons
history.text: The Confrérie des Vignerons of Vevey staged its first great festival on 9 August 1797. It is held about once a generation; the 2019 edition filled a 20,000-seat arena, and UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2016.

history.title: Phylloxera and mildew
history.text: Phylloxera and powdery mildew reached Switzerland in the late nineteenth century. The vineyard fell from about 33,000 ha at the end of the century to about 12,500 ha around 1960.

history.title: Merlot comes to Ticino
history.text: After phylloxera destroyed Ticino's old vineyards, Merlot from Bordeaux was planted from 1906 and became the canton's signature.

history.title: Cantonal AOCs
history.text: Geneva led the move to French-style cantonal appellations, and the Valais introduced the first cantonal quality hierarchy in 1990.

history.title: Lavaux becomes World Heritage
history.text: Lavaux, Vineyard Terraces, was inscribed by UNESCO in July 2007: about 830 hectares of terraces along 30 km of the north shore of Lake Geneva.

country.classification:
Appellations are cantonal. Each canton defines its AOC or AOCs, permitted grapes, yields and minimum sugar levels; federal law sets the framework. Most cantons have a single cantonal AOC (Genève, Valais, Neuchâtel, Ticino, Zürich, Schaffhausen, Graubünden and so on); Vaud divides itself into eight regional AOCs (Chablais, Lavaux, Calamin, Dézaley, La Côte, Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars and Vully), with communal names such as Yvorne, Aigle, Epesses, Saint-Saphorin, Féchy and Mont-sur-Rolle used inside them.

Grand Cru levels exist in several cantons. Vaud has two Grand Cru AOCs (Dézaley and Calamin) plus 'Premier Grand Cru' for individual estates, the Valais allows communes to define Grand Cru rules (Salgesch, Vétroz, Fully, Saint-Léonard and others), Geneva has Premier Cru communes, and the Neuchâtel and Three Lakes cantons have their own. Traditional names are protected locally: Fendant (Valais Chasselas), Dôle (a Valais red blend of Pinot Noir and Gamay), Salvagnin (a Vaud red blend), Oeil de Perdrix (Pinot Noir rosé, especially Neuchâtel), Johannisberg (Sylvaner in the Valais) and Malvoisie (Pinot Gris).
country.climate_soils:
Swiss vineyards are cool to moderate, but warmed by lakes and protected by mountains. Lake Geneva and the Jura lakes reflect light and store heat; the Valais lies in a deep rain shadow between the Bernese and Pennine Alps, with under 600 mm of rain in places and the warm föhn wind; Ticino has a sub-Mediterranean climate south of the Alps with heavy rain and sunshine.

Soils mirror Alpine geology: glacial moraine, limestone and conglomerate in Lavaux and Vaud, schist, gneiss, limestone and alluvial fans in the Valais, Jurassic limestone along Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel, molasse sandstone in the German-speaking cantons, and granite and gneiss with glacial deposits in Ticino.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: The most planted grape (about 3,950 ha), from the Bündner Herrschaft and Neuchâtel to the Valais.

grapes.name: Chasselas
grapes.note: About 3,650 ha; the soul of Vaud, called Fendant in the Valais, and a remarkable conduit for terroir.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.note: About 1,200 ha, mostly in Geneva, Vaud and the Valais.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: About 1,180 ha, the signature of Ticino since 1906.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau (Riesling x Sylvaner)
grapes.note: Bred at Geisenheim by Hermann Müller, a native of Thurgau, and the classic white of German-speaking Switzerland.

grapes.name: Petite Arvine
grapes.note: The Valais' signature white, salty and grapefruit-scented, dry or sweet.

grapes.name: Cornalin and Humagne Rouge
grapes.note: Native or ancient Valais reds; Cornalin (Rouge du Pays) is dark and cherry-fruited.

grapes.name: Heida (Savagnin)
grapes.note: Grown at over 1,100 m at Visperterminen in the Upper Valais.

grapes.name: Amigne
grapes.note: An ancient variety almost confined to Vétroz, made dry to sweet with a bee symbol showing sweetness.

grapes.name: Completer and Räuschling
grapes.note: Old German-Swiss rarities, Completer in Graubünden and Räuschling on Lake Zurich.

further_reading: Wine Grapes, Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz

regions.name: Valais
regions.tagline: A sun-trap valley of the Rhône with dozens of Alpine grapes and Europe's highest vineyards.
regions.summary:
The Valais is Switzerland's largest wine canton, with about 4,600 hectares, roughly a third of the national vineyard, stretched for about 100 km along the upper Rhône from Martigny to Visp. The valley lies in the rain shadow of high Alps on both sides, and the vineyards on the south-facing right bank, between 450 and 800 metres, are among the sunniest and driest places in the Alps. Irrigation channels called bisses, some centuries old, once carried glacier water across cliffs to the vines.

No other wine region of its size grows so many varieties. Chasselas, here called Fendant, and Pinot Noir dominate in volume, along with Gamay and the traditional red blend Dôle. But the Valais' fame now rests on its specialities: Petite Arvine (salty, rhubarb and grapefruit, from dry to late-harvest), Amigne from Vétroz, Humagne Blanche, Heida (Savagnin) from Visperterminen, Johannisberg (Sylvaner), Malvoisie (Pinot Gris, often sweet), Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Syrah, which has thrived on the warm slopes since the 1920s. In the Val d'Anniviers, villages such as Grimentz keep the Vin des Glaciers, an oxidative, solera-aged wine from the old Rèze grape kept in larch barrels.
regions.history: Celtic and Roman wine is attested here, from the Sembrancher bottle to Roman Octodurus (Martigny). The canton built its wine economy on Fendant for the Swiss market, then rebuilt its image from the 1990s around native grapes and quality rules; the 1990 cantonal quality hierarchy was Switzerland's first. Leading names include Marie-Thérèse Chappaz in Fully, Domaine Jean-René Germanier, Simon Maye, Denis Mercier, Provins (the big cooperative), Domaine Cornulus and Chanton in Visp.
regions.terroir: Schist, gneiss and limestone on steep right-bank slopes; alluvial fans and glacial deposits, often stony and well drained. Very dry (under 600 mm in parts), with intense sunlight, high diurnal range and the föhn wind.
regions.grapes: Chasselas (Fendant), Pinot Noir, Gamay, Petite Arvine, Syrah, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne, Heida, Johannisberg, Malvoisie, Chardonnay, Merlot.
regions.styles: Dry whites, light and serious reds, Dôle, sweet late-harvest and botrytised wines (Petite Arvine, Malvoisie, Amigne), Vin des Glaciers.
regions.classification: AOC Valais, with communal and local names and Grand Cru rules set by communes such as Salgesch, Vétroz, Fully and Saint-Léonard. Fendant and Dôle are protected traditional names.

regions.name: Vaud
regions.tagline: The terraces of Chasselas above Lake Geneva.
regions.summary:
Vaud, with about 3,800 hectares, is the heart of Chasselas and of Swiss wine culture. Its vineyards ring Lake Geneva from the city of Geneva's border to the Rhône delta and continue up the Rhône into the Chablais, with smaller areas near Lakes Neuchâtel and Murten. Chasselas covers most of the white vineyard, and the Vaudois approach is to let the grape transmit place: wines are named after villages and sites rather than grapes.

Four great areas define Vaud. Lavaux, between Lausanne and Vevey, is 830 hectares of terraces dropping to the lake, inscribed by UNESCO in 2007, with the Grand Cru appellations Dézaley and Calamin. The Chablais upstream, with Yvorne, Aigle, Ollon and Bex, has steeper, warmer slopes and gravelly soils. La Côte, between Lausanne and Nyon, is gentler and larger, with Féchy, Mont-sur-Rolle and Morges. Nord Vaudois (Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars, Vully) lies near the Jura lakes.
regions.history: Monks of the eleventh and twelfth centuries and the bishops of Lausanne built Lavaux's terraces; Bern ruled Vaud from 1536 to 1798, and after the Reformation church estates such as the Clos des Abbayes and Clos des Moines passed to the city of Lausanne, which still owns them. The Confrérie des Vignerons in Vevey has inspected vineyards and staged its festival since the eighteenth century.
regions.terroir: Glacial moraine, limestone, marl and conglomerate in Lavaux; scree and alluvial gravel in the Chablais; deeper moraine and molasse on La Côte. In Lavaux the 'three suns' (sky, lake reflection and warmth from the stone walls) ripen grapes on gradients of up to about 40 degrees.
regions.grapes: Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Gamaret, Garanoir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Merlot.
regions.styles: Dry Chasselas from light to deep and age-worthy, Salvagnin and Pinot-Gamay reds, some sparkling and sweet wines.
regions.classification: Eight cantonal AOCs: Chablais, Lavaux, Calamin (Grand Cru), Dézaley (Grand Cru), La Côte, Côtes de l'Orbe, Bonvillars and Vully (shared with Fribourg). Premier Grand Cru recognises individual estates. Communal names such as Yvorne, Aigle, Epesses, Saint-Saphorin, Féchy and Mont-sur-Rolle appear within the AOCs.

regions.name: Genève
regions.tagline: Switzerland's third canton, a flat crescent of Gamay and Chasselas around the city.
regions.summary: Geneva has about 1,340 hectares of vines, almost entirely surrounded by France, in three areas: the Mandement around Satigny (one of the largest wine communes in Switzerland), the land between the Arve and the Rhône, and between the Arve and the lake. The canton was the first to introduce French-style AOC rules in the late 1980s and is now a laboratory for new varieties: Gamaret and Garanoir (Swiss crossings of Gamay and Reichensteiner) do well here, and Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Merlot are all important. Premier Cru communes such as Satigny, Dardagny and Russin allow higher-grade labels.
regions.history: Monasteries and Geneva's merchants planted vines around the city from the Middle Ages. Today the canton's growers, including Domaine des Balisiers, Domaine de la Vigne Blanche and the Cave de Genève cooperative, have built a reputation for clean, modern wines.
regions.terroir: Glacial moraine and alluvial deposits on gentle slopes; a relatively warm, sunny climate moderated by the lake.
regions.grapes: Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamaret, Chardonnay, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc, Garanoir.
regions.styles: Dry whites and reds, rosé, sparkling.
regions.classification: AOC Genève with 22 Premier Cru areas.

regions.name: Three Lakes
regions.tagline: Pinot Noir, Oeil de Perdrix and Chasselas on Jurassic limestone.
regions.summary: Swiss Wine Promotion's Three Lakes region joins the vineyards along Lake Neuchâtel (canton of Neuchâtel, about 600 ha), Lake Biel (Bielersee, canton of Bern) and Lake Murten (Vully, shared by Fribourg and Vaud), about 945 hectares in all. The soils are Jurassic limestone like Burgundy's, and Pinot Noir and Chasselas dominate. Neuchâtel claims to have invented Oeil de Perdrix ('partridge eye'), a pale rosé of Pinot Noir, and is known for unfiltered Chasselas released in January. The Bielersee villages of Ligerz, Twann and Schafis grow Chasselas and Pinot on steep slopes above the lake.
regions.history: The Château d'Auvernier and the Château de Boudry (which houses a wine museum) recall Neuchâtel's long viticultural history under the Prussian kings, who ruled the principality until 1848.
regions.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl at the foot of the Jura, moraine and molasse at Vully; lakes moderate the climate.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chasselas, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Gamay.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, Oeil de Perdrix, Chasselas (including unfiltered), sparkling.
regions.classification: AOC Neuchâtel, AOC Bielersee (Lac de Bienne), AOC Vully (Vaud/Fribourg).

regions.name: Ticino
regions.tagline: Merlot under the palms, south of the Alps.
regions.summary: Ticino, Switzerland's Italian-speaking canton, has about 1,030 hectares of vines on hills and terraces from the Leventina to the Mendrisiotto near Como. After phylloxera wiped out the old local varieties, Merlot was planted from 1906 and now covers about 80 percent of the vineyard, giving everything from light reds to oak-aged wines of Bordeaux structure and, increasingly, white Merlot (vinified without skin contact). Rainfall is heavy but sunshine abundant, and the north (Sopraceneri, around Bellinzona and Locarno) has granite and gneiss while the south (Sottoceneri) has limestone and clay. Gialdi, Tamborini, Guido Brivio, Luigi Zanini's Castello di Morcote, Cantina Kopp von der Crone Visini and Christian Zündel are leading names.
regions.history: The canton has been growing wine since Roman times, but phylloxera ended the old tradition around 1900. In 2025 Ticino and Misox produced 3.4 million litres, down 8 percent, partly because of Japanese beetle in the Mendrisiotto.
regions.terroir: Granite, gneiss and glacial deposits north of Monte Ceneri; limestone, clay and moraine to the south; sub-Mediterranean climate with heavy rain.
regions.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bondola (a local survivor), Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.classification: AOC Ticino; the Ticino VITI label marks wines approved by a tasting panel.

sources.title: swissinfo.ch / FOAG: 2025 judged an excellent year for Swiss wine

regions.name: German-speaking Switzerland
regions.tagline: Small lake and valley vineyards, from Basel to the Bündner Herrschaft's Pinot Noir.
regions.summary: About 2,600 hectares of vines spread across 17 German-speaking cantons, from Basel and Aargau to Zurich, Schaffhausen, Thurgau, St. Gallen and Graubünden. Pinot Noir (Blauburgunder) is the main grape, and Müller-Thurgau, named after its Swiss breeder, the main white. The star is the Bündner Herrschaft in Graubünden, four villages (Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins and Malans) in the upper Rhine valley where the warm föhn wind ripens Pinot Noir of Burgundian finesse; Daniel and Martha Gantenbein, Georg Fromm, Thomas Studach and the Donatsch family make some of Switzerland's most sought-after reds. Graubünden is also home to Completer, an ancient white revived at Malans. Schaffhausen's Hallau and Zurich's lake villages make the bulk of the rest; the Wädenswil research station on Lake Zurich (now Agroscope) has its roots in the 1890 founding of an experimental station there.
regions.history: Monasteries and city councils spread the vine; Hermann Müller from Tägerwilen in Thurgau bred Müller-Thurgau at Geisenheim in 1882 and later directed Wädenswil. In 2025 German-speaking Switzerland's harvest rose by almost a third to 13.7 million litres.
regions.terroir: Molasse sandstone and marl, glacial moraine, limestone; föhn winds in Graubünden and the Rhine valley.
regions.grapes: Pinot Noir, Müller-Thurgau, Räuschling, Completer, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Blanc.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, light whites, some sparkling.
regions.classification: One cantonal AOC per canton (Graubünden, Zürich, Schaffhausen, Aargau, Thurgau, St. Gallen, Basel-Landschaft and others).

sources.title: swissinfo.ch / FOAG: 2025 judged an excellent year for Swiss wine

ch-aargau.name: Aargau
ch-aargau.summary: AOC Aargau has just under 400 hectares of vines on the Jura foothills and along the Aare, Limmat and Reuss, with Pinot Noir and Müller-Thurgau.

ch-bielersee.name: Bielersee
ch-bielersee.summary: The canton of Bern's lake appellation covers terraced vineyards along the north shore of Lake Biel at Ligerz, Twann, Schafis and La Neuveville and the island of St. Petersinsel. Chasselas and Pinot Noir grow on limestone below the Jura; the wine villages are among the prettiest in Switzerland. Bern also has a tiny vineyard on Lake Thun (AOC Thunersee).
ch-bielersee.terroir: Jurassic limestone on steep terraces above the lake.

ch-bonvillars.name: Bonvillars
ch-bonvillars.summary: A Vaud appellation on the north-west shore of Lake Neuchâtel around Grandson and Concise, where Jurassic limestone gives fresh Chasselas and Pinot Noir.
ch-bonvillars.terroir: Jurassic limestone at the foot of the Jura.

ch-calamin.name: Calamin
ch-calamin.summary: Calamin is the smallest Swiss AOC, about 16 hectares of terraces at Epesses in Lavaux, inside the commune next to Dézaley. Its deeper, clay-limestone soils, which slip slowly downhill, give a Chasselas that is fuller and more earthy than Dézaley.
ch-calamin.terroir: Clay-limestone moraine with landslide movement on steep terraces.
ch-calamin.nerd_note: The name may come from 'calamine', a zinc ore, or a local word for the area's clay soils.

ch-chablais.name: Chablais
ch-chablais.summary: AOC Chablais covers the Vaud vineyards of the upper Rhône valley between Lake Geneva and Saint-Maurice, with the communes of Villeneuve, Yvorne, Aigle, Ollon and Bex. Yvorne's vineyards grow on a massive landslide deposit of 1584, and Aigle's terraces surround a medieval castle that houses a wine museum. Chablais Chasselas is fuller and warmer than Lavaux's, with notes of flint and smoke.
ch-chablais.terroir: Scree, landslide debris, limestone and gypsum on the Rhône valley floor and slopes; warmed by the föhn.
ch-chablais.nerd_note: Henri Badoux's Aigle 'Les Murailles' label with its lizard is one of the best-known Swiss wine brands.

ch-cotes-de-l-orbe.name: Côtes de l'Orbe
ch-cotes-de-l-orbe.summary: A small Vaud appellation around Orbe and Arnex in the north of the canton, at the foot of the Jura, known for Chasselas, Pinot Noir and Gamay.

ch-dezaley.name: Dézaley
ch-dezaley.summary: Dézaley is a Grand Cru AOC of about 54 hectares on the steepest terraces of Lavaux, between Epesses and Rivaz, founded by Cistercian monks of Hautcrêt and Montheron in the twelfth century. Its Chasselas is the most powerful and long-lived in Switzerland, smoky and honeyed with age, and the city of Lausanne's Clos des Abbayes and Clos des Moines lie here. Dézaley Rouge is a rare red.
ch-dezaley.terroir: Conglomerate (poudingue) and marl on terraces facing due south above the lake.
ch-dezaley.nerd_note: A well-kept Dézaley can taste fresh after thirty years; the Bovard family has kept a vertical library going back decades.

ch-geneve.name: Genève
ch-geneve.grapes: Gamay, Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamaret, Chardonnay, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc
ch-geneve.summary: AOC Genève covers about 1,340 hectares around the city, in the Mandement (Satigny, Dardagny, Russin), between the Arve and the Rhône and between the Arve and the lake. Geneva pioneered cantonal AOC rules in Switzerland and has 22 Premier Cru areas. Gamay is the leading grape, with Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Gamaret and Garanoir, and the canton has a reputation for modern, well-made wines.
ch-geneve.terroir: Glacial moraine and alluvium on gentle slopes; sunny and relatively warm.
ch-geneve.nerd_note: Satigny is one of the largest wine-growing communes in Switzerland.

ch-graubunden.name: Graubünden
ch-graubunden.summary: AOC Graubünden covers vineyards mostly in the Bündner Herrschaft (Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins, Malans) on the upper Rhine, plus the Misox valley (south of the Alps, Merlot). The warm föhn wind ripens Pinot Noir of great elegance, and Malans keeps the ancient white Completer alive.

ch-la-cote.name: La Côte
ch-la-cote.summary: La Côte is Vaud's largest appellation, on gentle slopes between Lausanne and Nyon, with the communes of Morges, Aubonne, Féchy, Mont-sur-Rolle, Rolle, Begnins, Luins and Vinzel. Its Chasselas is light, fresh and easy, while Féchy and Mont-sur-Rolle give more structured examples, and Pinot Noir, Gamay and Gamaret are important reds.
ch-la-cote.terroir: Glacial moraine and molasse on broad, gentle slopes facing the lake and the Alps.
ch-la-cote.nerd_note: Raymond Paccot's biodynamic Domaine de la Colombe in Féchy is one of Switzerland's most respected estates.

ch-lavaux.name: Lavaux
ch-lavaux.summary: AOC Lavaux covers the terraced vineyards between Lausanne and Vevey (and up to Montreux), the most spectacular wine landscape in Switzerland and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007. About 830 hectares of walls and terraces drop steeply to Lake Geneva in the communes of Lutry, Villette, Epesses, Cully, Saint-Saphorin, Chexbres and Chardonne, around the two Grand Cru enclaves of Dézaley and Calamin. Chasselas is supreme, giving wines of floral delicacy at Lutry and of depth and minerality at Saint-Saphorin and Epesses.
ch-lavaux.terroir: Glacial moraine, marl, limestone and conglomerate on terraces with stone walls; the lake reflects light and warmth (the 'three suns').
ch-lavaux.nerd_note: A thirty-kilometre hiking route through the Lavaux terraces links the villages from Lutry to Chillon.

ch-neuchatel.name: Neuchâtel
ch-neuchatel.grapes: Chasselas, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris
ch-neuchatel.summary: AOC Neuchâtel covers about 600 hectares on Jurassic limestone along the north-west shore of Lake Neuchâtel, from Le Landeron to Vaumarcus, with Auvernier, Cortaillod and Boudry at its heart. Chasselas and Pinot Noir dominate. Neuchâtel's Oeil de Perdrix, a pale salmon rosé of Pinot Noir, is a local invention, and unfiltered Chasselas released on the third Wednesday of January is a cult.
ch-neuchatel.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl, like the Côte d'Or, under the Jura escarpment.
ch-neuchatel.nerd_note: Oeil de Perdrix is a protected name in Neuchâtel for Pinot Noir rosé.

ch-schaffhausen.name: Schaffhausen
ch-schaffhausen.summary: AOC Schaffhausen grows mostly Pinot Noir on limestone and molasse near the Rhine Falls; Hallau is the largest wine commune of German-speaking Switzerland.

ch-st-gallen.name: St. Gallen
ch-st-gallen.summary: AOC St. Gallen, mostly in the Rhine valley near the Austrian border, grows Pinot Noir in the warm föhn corridor.

ch-thurgau.name: Thurgau
ch-thurgau.summary: AOC Thurgau, home canton of Hermann Müller, grows Müller-Thurgau and Pinot Noir on about 250 hectares along the Thur and Lake Constance.

ch-ticino.name: Ticino
ch-ticino.summary: AOC Ticino covers about 1,030 hectares in the Italian-speaking canton, split by Monte Ceneri into the Sopraceneri (granite, around Bellinzona, Locarno and the Gudo and Giubiasco slopes) and the Sottoceneri (limestone and clay, around Lugano and Mendrisio). Merlot, planted since 1906, is the defining grape, from fresh, cherry-scented reds to Bordeaux-like reserve wines, plus white Merlot. The VITI label marks wines approved by a tasting panel.
ch-ticino.terroir: Granite and gneiss north of Monte Ceneri, limestone and moraine south; humid, sunny, sub-Mediterranean.
ch-ticino.nerd_note: Bondola, a local red grape that survived phylloxera, is still made by a few growers as a curiosity.

ch-valais.name: Valais
ch-valais.created: 1990 (cantonal quality hierarchy); AOC rules updated since
ch-valais.grapes: Chasselas (Fendant), Pinot Noir, Gamay, Petite Arvine, Syrah, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne, Heida and many others
ch-valais.summary: The cantonal AOC of the Valais covers about 4,600 hectares along the upper Rhône and is the most varied appellation in Switzerland, with dozens of permitted varieties. It contains famous communal names (Fully, Chamoson, Vétroz, Conthey, Sion, Saint-Léonard, Sierre, Salgesch, Leuk, Visperterminen) and Grand Cru rules defined commune by commune. Fendant (Chasselas) and Dôle (a blend in which Pinot Noir dominates, with Gamay) are the classics, but Petite Arvine, Cornalin, Humagne Rouge, Amigne and Heida have made the canton internationally interesting. Chamoson is the largest wine commune of the Valais and a Johannisberg (Sylvaner) stronghold; Fully, on a granite fan, is the capital of Petite Arvine and Gamay; Salgesch, at the language border, is known for Pinot Noir.
ch-valais.terroir: Schist, gneiss, limestone and alluvial fans on steep slopes in a dry, sunny valley.
ch-valais.nerd_note: The Valais has a bee-shaped sweetness scale for Amigne de Vétroz: one bee is dry, three bees sweet.

ch-vully.name: Vully
ch-vully.summary: Vully is the vineyard on the slopes of Mont Vully between Lake Murten and Lake Neuchâtel, shared by Vaud and Fribourg, and part of the Three Lakes region. Chasselas, Pinot Noir and the aromatic Traminer are the main wines.
ch-vully.nerd_note: Vully is one of the few Swiss AOCs that crosses a cantonal border.

ch-zurich.name: Zürich
ch-zurich.summary: AOC Zürich covers about 640 hectares on the shores of Lake Zurich and in the Zürcher Weinland near Schaffhausen. Pinot Noir (Blauburgunder), Müller-Thurgau and the old local white Räuschling dominate.

sites.name: Dézaley
sites.text: The terraces of Dézaley, founded by Cistercian monks in the twelfth century, drop to the lake between Epesses and Rivaz. Chasselas here is the richest and longest-lived in Switzerland.

sites.name: Calamin
sites.text: Sixteen hectares of slowly slipping clay-limestone terraces at Epesses, the smallest AOC in Switzerland; its Chasselas is earthy and full.

sites.name: Clos des Abbayes
sites.text: A walled vineyard owned by the city of Lausanne since the Reformation, when it took over church property from the Cistercians; its annual auction is a Lavaux event.

sites.name: Clos des Moines
sites.text: The neighbouring clos owned by the city of Lausanne, also a former monastic vineyard, at Treytorrens in the Dézaley; like the Clos des Abbayes its wine is sold at an annual city auction.

sites.name: Lavaux Vinorama
sites.text: A wine centre at Rivaz at the foot of the Dézaley that sells and pours wines from all Lavaux producers and tells the region's story.

sites.name: Lavaux terraces (UNESCO)
sites.text: About 830 hectares of terraced vineyards on 30 km of Lake Geneva's north shore, built by monks from the eleventh century and inscribed by UNESCO as 'Lavaux, Vineyard Terraces' in 2007.

sites.name: Fête des Vignerons, Vevey
sites.text: Vevey's market square hosts the Fête des Vignerons, staged by the Confrérie des Vignerons since 1797, about once a generation. The 2019 edition had a 20,000-seat arena and some 6,000 performers.

sites.name: Château de Chillon
sites.text: The famous lakeside castle near Montreux has its own small vineyard, the Clos de Chillon, and wine has been stored in its vaults for centuries.

sites.name: Yvorne
sites.text: A Chablais village whose vineyards lie on the debris of a great landslide in 1584; its Chasselas is famous for its flinty, smoky character.

sites.name: Château d'Aigle (Musée de la Vigne et du Vin)
sites.text: A medieval castle among vineyards above Aigle that houses the Vaud wine museum and a wine-label museum.

sites.name: Féchy
sites.text: A La Côte village known for structured Chasselas, home of Raymond Paccot's biodynamic Domaine de la Colombe.

sites.name: Mont-sur-Rolle
sites.text: One of the largest wine communes of Vaud, on slopes above Rolle facing the lake and Mont Blanc.

sites.name: Visperterminen (Riebe vineyards)
sites.text: Terraced vineyards climbing from about 650 to over 1,100 metres above Visp, often called among the highest in Europe, planted with Heida (Savagnin). The St. Jodern cooperative and the 'Heidadorf' village make it a pilgrimage for Alpine wine. Coordinates mark the village.

sites.name: Salgesch
sites.text: A wine village at the French-German language border in the Valais, known for Pinot Noir and its own Grand Cru rules; it shares the Valais wine museum with Sierre.

sites.name: Château de Villa (Musée valaisan de la Vigne et du Vin)
sites.text: A sixteenth-century manor in Sierre housing the Valais wine museum's oenothèque and a restaurant famous for raclette; the museum's second site is in Salgesch, linked by a vineyard trail.

sites.name: Chamoson
sites.class: Largest wine commune of the Valais
sites.text: A broad alluvial fan below the Haut de Cry, the Valais' largest wine commune and a stronghold of Johannisberg (Sylvaner).

sites.name: Fully
sites.text: A granite slope at the bend of the Rhône below Martigny, famous for Petite Arvine, Gamay and Marie-Thérèse Chappaz's biodynamic sweet wines.

sites.name: Vétroz
sites.text: The village that holds most of the world's tiny plantings of Amigne, labelled with one to three bees for sweetness.

sites.name: Château d'Auvernier
sites.text: A sixteenth-century château and the largest private estate in Neuchâtel, run by the Montmollin family for generations.

sites.name: Château de Boudry
sites.text: A medieval castle housing the Musée de la vigne et du vin of Neuchâtel and the Compagnie des Vignolants wine brotherhood.

sites.name: Ligerz
sites.text: A wine village on the steep north shore of Lake Biel, with a vineyard museum and a hillside church among the vines.

sites.name: Fläsch
sites.text: The northernmost village of the Bündner Herrschaft, home of Gantenbein, whose Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are among Switzerland's most coveted.

sites.name: Maienfeld
sites.text: The 'Heidi' town of the Bündner Herrschaft, centre of Pinot Noir in Graubünden, home of Schloss Salenegg, one of the oldest wine estates in Switzerland.

sites.name: Malans
sites.class: Bündner Herrschaft village, home of Completer
sites.text: The village where the ancient Completer grape survived, now made by Donatsch and others; also fine Pinot Noir from Georg Fromm and Thomas Studach.

sites.name: Agroscope Wädenswil
sites.text: The federal research station on Lake Zurich, on Müller-Thurgau-Strasse, heir to the 1890 Wädenswil fruit and wine institute where Hermann Müller worked.

sites.name: Weinbaumuseum am Zürichsee
sites.text: A wine museum in Au near Wädenswil with historic presses, on a peninsula of vineyards above Lake Zurich.

sites.name: Hallau
sites.text: The largest wine commune of German-speaking Switzerland, a sea of Pinot Noir around a hilltop church.

sites.name: Gudo
sites.text: A village on the sunny right bank of the Ticino plain near Bellinzona whose granite terraces give fine Merlot.

sites.name: Mendrisio
sites.text: The wine capital of the southern Ticino, centre of the Mendrisiotto vineyards on limestone and clay, hit by Japanese beetle in 2025.
